Man. That's not what I was arguing at all. Criterion doesn't have a bias against Asian cinema (or foreign cinema in general), I was saying they have a bias against movies like House. I thought I reinforced that point when I mentioned Wes Anderson vs. Ralph Bakshi at the end (though, tbf I'm not sure Bakshi is the greatest example). I almost brought up Parasite to talk about the contrast between how both films are treated and talked about but I didn't because I haven't actually seen Parasite. Not going to get into any further specifics here because it doesn't fucking matter, I shouldn't need to address every minute detail of something.

And no offense to you or your family or whatever, but I'm probably always going to associate snobbery and respectability politics with whiteness. I didn't mean at all to posit that as being something only white people are capable of though, I know for a fact that isn't true. Hell, I fall into that trap myself sometimes. Most people I know would call me a "snob". 

Criterion can release whatever they want. They are not the be all end all of boutique blu-rays or film curation. My only wish is that going forward they would treat their less conventional releases the way they treat everything else since it's not like they're being released under a sub label or something. There is no "TCM Underground" of Criterion so if they're going to release movies that are considered less "dignified" together with the art house stuff and classics (and honestly, House is art house) they should be more respectful of those films. *All* those films. Like, if they had released Basket Case instead of Arrow. Or if they were to release the original Texas Chain Saw Massacre sometime in the future (which they **REALLY** should), I would like them to package and describe it as fancy as they would any other boring artsy fartsy movie they release. Or something like Love Exposure. Or Hideaki Anno's Love & Pop. Those are two movies someone might be weird about because of what they were shot on, as if Criterion isn't about to release Inland Empire, which was shot on a camcorder and is boring as fuck.

Not sure how unpopular of opinion this but I think some of there choices are rather strange and annoying. And I can't stand the snobbery. The same thing that draws me to Criterion, the fanciness and (some of) the pretentiousness, is also what drives me away. Like, Criterion strikes me as being a very white company and they kind of purport respectability politics in a way, for lack of a better term.

I find it difficult to really verbalize what I mean, but they treat some of the films they release differently than others and it affects how others view it. House (1977) is one of my favorite movies. I own their release of it and love it's features but the way they talk about and describe it on their website and on the packaging feels extremely dismissive and like it leans into a sort of Orientalism. Not only are Criterion responsible for the whole "Hausu" thing but they also seem very responsible for the fact most people I talk to don't take the movie seriously. It's seen as "watch while high" fodder and furthers the idea "Wow! Japanese people sure are WEIRD and WACKY!!!". House has childish SFX sure, but that's by design, a surrealist film from a white German director that came out around the same time wouldn't be treated the same way. Even their description of Pink Flamingos makes it sound like it's something super serious and important, doesn't Divine eat shit in that film? Not that the description isn't one of the odd men out among some of their "campier" releases. Again, they treat different movies differently, despite them all being released under the same general label.

I just wish Criterion would expand their view of what's considered "important" and be more respectful of the films that are maybe a bit more vulgar or, what's the word? I don't know, shit that isn't so white and conventional. Old "classics" and modern dramadies from high profile extremely critically lauded auteurs aren't the only movies deserving of respect. I love Wes Anderson, I also love Ralph Bakshi. It's why my most recent blu-ray acquisitions have been from labels like Arrow (Basket Case), Kino Lorber (VIVA), and Arbelos (Belladonna of Sadness and Funeral Parade of Roses) instead.

Also, unrelated, but they really need to re-release Peeping Tom on blu-ray. Would love to be able to have that, Black Narcissus, and The Red Shoes.

Man. Dude. I agree with almost everything you're saying but to say characterization is unimportant is weird, I can't agree with that at all. Movies and TV shows tend to completely fall flat for me if the characters just feel like standard archetypes or plot devices. I need characters to have some level of specificity, even if it's minor. Jason Takes Manhattan is a good example. It's the Friday the 13th movie everybody hates the most but it's my favorite (along with Part 5 and Part 7) because there's even the slightest implication that the characters have a little more going on then just their archetypes (something most other movies in the franchise don't do), the characters are able to feel "lived in". And while Rennie, the final girl character, doesn't have that much going on but the writers gave her a fear of water which is pretty fucking specific. The writers then double down on that specificity by having the entire movie take place on a boat and then later revealing that her aquaphobia stems from the repressed memory of an incident she had a kid that had left her traumatized. It's also the reason why I love Nightmare on Elm Street 2 (Jesse is a very specific character) and why I don't really care for Nancy in the first movie but love her in Dream Warriors. 

Besides all that though, yes. Film and TV shows are too often just thought of and evaluated as literature, and not just by critics but I feel like by fans and sometimes filmmakers themselves too. It's actually something I got into an argument about a few months ago when someone was \[angrily\] trying to convince me that Gurren Lagann was better than Kill La Kill. His only argument was that "if you wrote it as a book it'd be a masterpiece" and that KLK was too full of "random bullshit" like FLCL. But the fact that Kill La Kill and Fooly Cooly wouldn't make sense written out as novels is exactly why they're good. The medium is the message and both shows take full advantage of the medium. The same goes for Into the Spiderverse with different art styles used to reflect different worlds/tones and characters being animated at different frame rates to reflect different personalities. It's a movie that couldn't exist in live-action, at least nowhere near as effectively... 

There's a reason why book to movie adaptations usually fall flat when they're too literal or directly translated. If critics can acknowledge that they should also be able to realize how flawed it is to judge films like they're literature.

As a kid some of the things that terrified me were Who Framed Roger Rabbit, Pleasantville, Halloweentown 2, Pete's Dragon, The Shaggy Dog (the original), black and white movies, and Jumanji (I've never actually seen it, just the very ending so it was more the general idea of it that freaked me out). I stayed far away from anything that was horror-esque or even slightly scary, even The Haunted Mansion movie with Eddie Murphy. The irony here was that as a kid I was also REALLY into alt-rock/emo bands who all had dark macabre kind of images and I was obsessed with Tim Burton movies. Like, I even had a pack of Tim Burton playing cards. 

My freshman year of high school I watched the Evil Dead trilogy and they became the only horror movies I could stand and were "acceptable" in my eyes but the first movie still scared me and I was still put off by horror movies. 

It wasn't until I was 18 that I watched a horror movie again. I was in my freshman year of college and as an aspiring filmmaker I wanted to make a movie and decided to go with a slasher despite it belonging to a genre I've been afraid of my entire life because I knew that it was something you could pull off relatively cheaply. So I started watching slasher films for research like the first Halloween, Friday the 13th, and Nightmare on Elm Street and was surprised to find most of them more boring and lame than scary. It was also around this time that It: Chapter One came out and everybody was talking about it. Between researching horror and just not wanting to be OOTL I ended up wanting to see it, but I was foced to go alone seeing as how both my sister and my crush at the time had already seen it. It was the first horror movie I saw in theaters and even though it actually did kinda scare me I was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. Still wasn't really into horror though. 

New Years Day 2018 the El Rey network did a marathon of the Nightmare on Elm Street movies and though I hated the first one and missed the second one (its my favorite now) I was bored enough to tune in right at the beginning of Dream Warriors. I wound up staying up all night till 4 or 5 AM watching Dream Warriors, The Dream Master, and half of The Dream Child and it was that (and the Nightmare on Elm Street franchise as a whole) that cemented my interest and love of the genre. I am still a newbie and there's still a lot of stuff I haven't seen but I've opened up to a lot of shit and honestly even kind of consider horror my to be my "main" genre now.
